title: Chapter 9. Of the Several Subjects of Knowledge
paragraphs:
_Knowledge_

Knowledge is of two kinds. One is knowledge of fact; the other is knowledge of the consequence of one affirmation to another. The first is nothing but sense and memory, and it is absolute knowledge — as when we see a fact being done, or remember it as done; this is the kind of knowledge required of a witness. The second is called science, and it is conditional — as when we know that if the figure shown is a circle, then any straight line through its centre divides it into two equal parts. This is the kind of knowledge required of a philosopher: that is, of anyone who claims to be reasoning.

The record of knowledge of fact is called history. There are two sorts. The first is natural history, which is the history of those facts, or effects of nature, that do not depend on the will of man — such as the histories of metals, plants, animals, regions, and the like. The second is civil history, which is the history of the voluntary actions of men in commonwealths.

The records of science are the books that contain the demonstrations of the consequences of one affirmation to another; these are commonly called books of philosophy. They are of many sorts, according to the variety of subject matter, and may be divided in the way I have divided them in the table that follows.
I. Science — that is, knowledge of consequences; also called PHILOSOPHY.
A. Consequences from the accidents of natural bodies; which is called NATURAL PHILOSOPHY.
1. Consequences from the accidents common to all natural bodies, namely quantity and motion.

a. Consequences of indeterminate quantity and motion, which are the principles or first foundation of philosophy: PHILOSOPHIA PRIMA, first philosophy.

b. Consequences of determinate motion and quantity:
1) Consequences of quantity and motion determined by figure or number: mathematics, GEOMETRY and ARITHMETIC.
2) Consequences of the motion and quantity of particular bodies:
a) Of the great parts of the world, such as the earth and stars: cosmography, ASTRONOMY and GEOGRAPHY.
b) Of particular kinds and shapes of bodies: mechanics, the doctrine of weight, ENGINEERING, ARCHITECTURE and NAVIGATION.

2. PHYSICS, or consequences of qualities:

a. Consequences of the qualities of transient bodies, which sometimes appear and sometimes vanish: METEOROLOGY.

b. Consequences of the qualities of permanent bodies:
1) Of the qualities of the stars:
a) Of the light of the stars. From this and the motion of the sun comes SCIOGRAPHY, the science of shadows.
b) Of the influence of the stars: ASTROLOGY.

2) Consequences of the qualities of fluid bodies that fill the space between the stars, such as air or ethereal substance.

3) Consequences of the qualities of terrestrial bodies:
a) Of parts of the earth without sense:
1] Of minerals, such as stones, metals and the like.
2] Of plants.
b) Of animals:
1] Of animals in general:
a] Of vision: OPTICS.
b] Of sounds: MUSIC.
c] Of the other senses.
2] Of human beings in particular:
a] Of human passions: ETHICS.
b] Of speech:
i) In praising, disparaging and the like: POETRY.
ii) In persuading: RHETORIC.
iii) In reasoning: LOGIC.
iv) In contracting: the science of JUST and UNJUST.
B. Consequences from the accidents of political bodies; which is called POLITICS, and CIVIL PHILOSOPHY.
1. Of consequences from the institution of COMMONWEALTHS, leading to the rights and duties of the body politic, or sovereign.
2. Of consequences from the same, leading to the duty and right of the subjects.
